# SaaS integrations, callbacks, and webhooks

- Use a maintained official client or a small well-reviewed HTTP integration. Request only the scopes, tenant access, events, and data fields the feature requires.
- Store OAuth client secrets, refresh tokens, API keys, webhook secrets, and certificates in the approved secret manager. Encrypt sensitive tokens at rest and design rotation/revocation without downtime.
- Validate the provider/tenant/issuer and exact redirect URI. Bind OAuth `state`/PKCE and callback data to the initiating user session; prevent account-linking and cross-tenant confusion.
- Verify webhook authenticity over the exact raw request bytes using the provider's current signature scheme. Check timestamp tolerance, constant-time signature comparison, expected event source, and secret version.
- Prevent replay with a provider event ID or nonce stored atomically for an appropriate window. Make handlers idempotent and queue work only after authentication and basic bounds checks.
- Treat webhook and SaaS response fields as untrusted. Validate schema, allowed event types, object ownership, URLs, filenames, and downstream rendering/query contexts.
- Do not infer authorization from possession of an external object ID. Map external tenant/user identities to an approved internal binding and reauthorize each resulting action.
- Use strict outbound destination configuration; do not accept arbitrary user-supplied base URLs for a privileged integration. Apply TLS verification, timeouts, response-size limits, bounded retry, and egress controls.
- Minimize transferred personal/sensitive data and avoid copying the provider's entire payload into logs or databases. Define retention, deletion, residency, and failure/reconciliation behavior.
- Fail closed on signature, token, tenant, or schema errors. Monitor authentication failures, permission changes, delivery gaps, and repeated poison events without leaking secrets.
